candidates.attacker_control: An attacker who can supply or influence bytes that are deserialized into a DiskFileItem (FileItem extends Serializable; DiskFileItem was made serializable in an earlier release) controls the serialized fields repository, dfosFile, cachedContent and sizeThreshold. This is the standard untrusted-deserialization trust boundary; the library itself exposes the gadget behavior in readObject.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether the repository validation exists elsewhere: search for isDirectory/InvalidObjectException found nothing; readObject contains no check. Checked whether the original filename is attacker-used for the write: DiskFileItem.getName() applies Streams.checkFileName (NUL check) and the write uses a generated upload_<UID>_<counter>.tmp name, so the written file name is not freely attacker-chosen; this limits but does not remove the write impact. Checked changes.xml: the 1.3.1 security note for this hardening is present with date TBD while the code change is absent, indicating the snapshot predates the fix. Did not find any compensating validation in getOutputStream/getTempFile/write.
candidates.impact: Integrity/availability impact on the server host: deletion of a file whose path the attacker chose in the serialized object, plus creation of an attacker-content file (generated name, attacker-chosen directory) which can overwrite/plant files in directories writable by the server and, depending on deployment, contribute to further compromise (e.g., writing attacker data into a web-accessible or watched directory). Content of the attacker-chosen dfosFile is also copied into the generated upload file.
candidates.prerequisites: The hosting application must deserialize attacker-influenced data as a DiskFileItem (e.g., file items persisted/cached/serialized in a session or distributed cache and later deserialized). No other precondition is needed inside the library; the vulnerable code path runs on the first write/close in readObject.
candidates.root_cause: DiskFileItem.readObject() calls in.defaultReadObject() and then immediately uses the deserialized fields without validating them: `repository` (File) is used as the directory for a newly created temp file via getOutputStream()->getTempFile(), `cachedContent` (byte[]) is written to that file, and `dfosFile` (File) is opened with FileInputStream and then deleted. There is no check that repository is null or an existing directory, and no check that dfosFile is a legitimate temp file. changes.xml lines 46-50 show the project considered this exact hardening necessary for 1.3.1, yet the code contains no such validation (search for isDirectory/InvalidObjectException returns nothing).
candidates.title: DiskFileItem deserialization trusts repository/dfosFile/cachedContent, enabling attacker-directed file write, read and deletion
candidates.trace: readObject (654-671) -> in.defaultReadObject() restores repository/dfosFile/cachedContent/sizeThreshold -> getOutputStream() (525-532) -> getTempFile() (578-590) builds new File(repository != null ? repository : java.io.tmpdir, "upload_<UID>_<counter>.tmp") -> DeferredFileOutputStream(sizeThreshold, outputFile) -> if cachedContent != null, output.write(cachedContent) persists attacker bytes into a file inside the attacker-chosen directory; else new FileInputStream(dfosFile) reads an attacker-chosen path, copies it into the temp file and dfosFile.delete() deletes the attacker-specified file. Nothing validates the repository directory or the dfosFile path.
candidates.unverified: Runtime exploitation was not performed and no application-level deserialization sink exists in this repository, so the untrusted-deserialization precondition is external and unproven here. Exact behavior of DeferredFileOutputStream threshold vs. cachedContent size (whether a disk file is materialized for small payloads) was reasoned from source only; the serialized final sizeThreshold field is assumed restorable by defaultReadObject. Whether this snapshot is the exact parent of the upstream CVE-2013-2186 fix commit is inferred from changes.xml, not from history metadata (no VCS data in the snapshot).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data (insecure deserialization leading to arbitrary file write/delete)

coverage_summary: Reviewed all 51 main Java files at least by listing/search and read the core files in full or in large parts: MultipartStream.java (1030 lines), DiskFileItem.java (689 lines), FileUploadBase.java (read key regions: boundary extraction 419-436, FileItemIteratorImpl 930-1120), util/Streams.java, plus targeted searches across the tree (Serializable, ObjectInputStream, isDirectory, repository, tempFile, boundary). The P1 relation index is partial (51 Java files, only 12 parsed; no control-flow or data-flow analysis, 846 unresolved calls), so it was used only for navigation and every candidate was re-verified against source text. Tests were inspected selectively (MultipartStreamTest, FileUploadTestCase) and contain no regression test for either candidate. Site/build files were checked only for version dating (pom 1.4-SNAPSHOT, commons-io 2.2, site advertises 1.3).
limitations: No runtime, build, or exploit execution; findings are static source conclusions only.

P1 index coverage is partial (12 of 51 Java files parsed; no data_flow/control_flow support; 846 unresolved calls), so cross-file reachability and application-side deserialization sinks could not be established from the index.
Only this repository's source is visible; the surrounding web application that would perform deserialization (trust boundary for the DiskFileItem candidate) is not part of the snapshot.
Version/history dating relies on pom.xml, changes.xml (1.3.1 date=TBD) and site pages; no VCS metadata is present, so the exact upstream commit and CVE mapping are inferred, not confirmed.
Other files (portlet/servlet adapters, util/mime decoders, deprecated DefaultFileItem/DiskFileUpload) were not read line-by-line; they are secondary to the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: MultipartStream accepts an unbounded boundary length and ItemInputStream.makeAvailable() can spin forever on zero-length reads (MultipartStream.java constructor 323-344 has no boundary vs. bufSize validation; makeAvailable loop 996-1016 calls input.read(buffer, tail, bufSize - tail) with len==0 once tail==bufSize and pad==bufSize, which returns 0 forever).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible remote DoS (a Content-Type boundary longer than ~4092 bytes with a >=4096-byte body), and the mechanism traces cleanly through source, but it was not selected because only one candidate may be submitted and the repository's own changes.xml security entry points at the DiskFileItem deserialization path missing its fix; also not runtime-verified and no equivalent security note exists for it in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: File name handling in Streams.checkFileName / InvalidFileNameException.
rejected_leads.reason: The NUL-character check is present and wired into DiskFileItem.getName(); no missing-validation evidence found.
HEADER_PART_SIZE_MAX check is present (MultipartStream.java 538-542); only a stale TODO in the javadoc, which is a documentation smell, not a vulnerability.
Limits are enforced in FileItemIteratorImpl (963-981) and LimitedInputStream; no bypass found in the inspected paths.

summary: Reviewed the Apache Commons FileUpload 1.4-SNAPSHOT tree (75 visible files; no reference to any external data). The strongest source-supported candidate is in disk/DiskFileItem.java: the private readObject() restores serialization-controlled fields (repository, dfosFile, cachedContent, sizeThreshold) and then unconditionally creates a temp file in the deserialized `repository` directory, writes deserialized `cachedContent` into it, or opens and deletes the deserialized `dfosFile` path, with no validation at all. The repository's own changes.xml (1.3.1 section, date TBD) records that this exact deserialization path was supposed to be hardened ("ensure that the repository location, if any, is a valid one"), but no such check exists anywhere in the snapshot (no isDirectory/InvalidObjectException use). I selected this over an equally plausible MultipartStream resource-exhaustion lead (unvalidated boundary length causing a zero-length read spin), because the repository-intrinsic security note plus the missing validation together give the strongest source evidence.
